summary: Discovery focused on per-token economics for a recommendation and chat augmentation workload. Key concerns: predictable monthly spend, EU data residency, bursty traffic, and tradeoffs between hosted, dedicated, and private. Redwood AE/SE explained batching/caching levers, quantization options, and fallback routing. Agreed next steps: send cost workbook, security docs, and schedule technical benchmark session.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-26 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Sarah (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Maya (Bluehaven Head of ML), Liam (CTO), Evelyn (Security Lead)

[00:00] Sarah: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick intros?
[00:10] Maya: Hi, Maya here. Head of ML at Bluehaven. We run recommendations and an in-product assistant, both chaty and embed-style use cases.
[00:18] Liam: Liam, CTO. I'm mostly here for infra constraints and cost visibility.
[00:23] Evelyn: Evelyn, security. Data residency and KMS are my primary bits.
[00:30] Sarah: Great. Carlos is our solutions engineer, he does the deep cost/lats stuff.
[00:36] Carlos: Hi all. Quick agenda: understanding your traffic and SLOs, walk through levers (batching, KV cache, quantization), and map hosted/dedicated/private tradeoffs.

[01:05] Maya: To ground this — our current monthly active users are ~80k, peak concurrent requests in a burst pattern (3x around product launches). Typical prompt is 400 tokens in, 120 tokens out for recommendations + explanation.
[01:22] Liam: We have a hard budget ceiling for POC: $20k/month for inference initially; long-term runway if unit economics look good.
[01:30] Evelyn: And EU data residency is mandatory for a subset of customers — so we need to understand where data sits with each deployment option and encryption at rest/key control.

[02:10] Carlos: Good, that's helpful. Roughly, per-token hosted pricing gives predictability for small scale but can blow up. Dedicated gives predictable throughput and lower per-token when you amortize the GPU pool. Private/VPC gives you residency and KMS control but ops overhead plus fixed costs.

[03:00] Sarah: We're going to walk through a simple per-100k-token example to make tradeoffs visible — and then point out levers. Any red lines?
[03:10] Liam: If we can't guarantee residency for those EU tenants, we can't use hosted for them.
[03:15] Evelyn: Correct. Also, we need audit logs for requests and token-level costing breakdown for chargebacks internally.

[04:05] Carlos: On levers — batching: if your average RTT allows, grouping requests into micro-batches reduces per-token compute. KV cache/prefix caching: for recommendation flows with repeated context or session state, caching KV reduces re-tokenization and model compute. Quantization: moving from FP16 to INT8 or 4-bit variants can reduce cost by 30-60% depending on model and accuracy tolerance.

[05:00] Maya: Quick question — our prompts vary a lot; can batching still help? During peaks, we have many similar short requests for top-k items, but the chat assistant has longer contexts.
[05:12] Carlos: Yes. For short, high-QPS calls, batching is very effective. For long context chat, KV cache helps more. You can also hybridize routes: route short, latency-tolerant queries to a high-batch pool; route low-latency chat to a dedicated low-latency pool — Redwood supports policy-based routing and fallbacks.

[06:05] Liam: Any numbers on expected savings from batching + KV? Ballpark.
[06:10] Carlos: Ballpark — micro-batching 8-16 items can drop per-token cost ~20-35% depending on overhead. KV cache for repeated prefixes can cut 10-40% on token compute. Combined, optimistic cases see 40-60% lower token spend compared to naive single-request serving. But that is workload dependent.

[07:00] Maya: Sounds promising. What about dedicated pricing — how should we think about committed capacity vs burst?
[07:10] Sarah: Dedicated is reservation-based. You commit to a GPU pool for a period (monthly/annual), which gives you lower per-token when utilized. We also offer burst capacity to handle spikes. If your utilization is low, though, it might cost more than hosted per-token.
[07:35] Liam: So for our POC budget ($20k/month), do you think dedicated is feasible?
[07:42] Carlos: Depends on the model and utilization. For example, a single A100 pool sized for your bursts may cost $Xk/month; if you run steady throughput to use most capacity, you'll get favorable per-token. But if 80% of cost is unused time, hosted might be cheaper for the POC. We'll model it in the spreadsheet.

[08:50] Evelyn: For private/VPC, can we bring our own key management and have logs exported to our SIEM?
[08:58] Sarah: Yes — private offers customer-managed KMS and audit log exports. On-prem package is also possible for air-gapped customers, but that's a longer procurement cycle.

[09:30] Maya: One thing: we can't accept model outputs leaving EU for those customers. How strict is your routing by region?
[09:37] Carlos: We support region pinning and policy routing. For EU-residency requests, we can pin to EU hosts only. If pooled capacity in EU is full, Redwood can fail closed or fall back to a compatible model hosted in EU — we don't route EU payloads to NA unless allowed.

[10:20] Liam: Good. Let's talk models — are we talking open models or proprietary? We currently use a mix: some open Llama-derived models in prod experiments, and occasionally API-based large models for high-quality outputs.
[10:30] Sarah: Redwood supports both open and tuned variants; we also have verified performance profiles per model. Note: quantization support varies by model and may affect latency.

[11:15] Maya: Example: for our recommendation explainers, 95% of calls use a 2k-context model? No, sorry — incorrect. Let me rephrase: typical long assistant contexts are ~2k tokens occasionally, but most are under 1k.
[11:30] Carlos: That's useful. Sequence length distribution matters — longer contexts increase KV pressure and latency, and also change kernel selection.

[12:05] Sarah: Let's sketch a concrete scenario in the workbook: 100k requests/day, average 520 tokens per request (in+out). We'll calculate hosted per-token vs dedicated amortized. We'll include batching scenarios (no batch, batch=8, batch=16) and quantization options.

[13:30] Maya: Can you also include end-to-end latency SLOs in the sheet? We care about p95 under 300ms for chat on mobile.
[13:40] Carlos: We'll add latency columns: p50/p95 and the expected tradeoffs when batching. If p95 latency needs to be <300ms, certain batching sizes won't be acceptable for chat, but they may be for recommendations.

[14:20] Liam: Curious about caching TTLs — if we cache per-session KV, what is the storage cost and how much does that save compute?
[14:28] Carlos: Storage for KV cache is relatively cheap compared to compute, but it depends on model KV size (per token). In many cases, storing session prefixes yields large compute reductions. We'll surface an estimated cache hit rate and impact in the workbook.

[15:45] Evelyn: Audit logs — are token-level logs included for private deployments? Any PII redaction options?
[15:55] Sarah: For private/VPC, you control redaction. By default hosted logs keep minimal request metadata and not full payloads unless enabled. We can support redaction rules and hashing of PII before storage. We'll send the SOC2 and security sheet.

[17:10] Maya: Another practical question — our engineers prefer not to change a lot of inference code. How much instrumentation does Redwood require to enable batching/cache?
[17:22] Carlos: Minimal SDK changes in most cases — we provide SDKs with automatic batching toggles and cache hooks. For advanced use you can implement policy tags per request for routing. We'll show sample code in the follow-up.

[18:30] Liam: Let's talk concrete numbers briefly — don't need the workbook to be perfect now, but give me a rough hosted price for 1M tokens and a dedicated amortized price for 1M tokens at ~70% utilization on an A100 pool.
[18:42] Carlos: Off the cuff: hosted could be $X per 1M tokens (we'll fill number in workbook) — dedicated at 70% utilization often ends up 30-50% cheaper per token, depending on batch/quantization. The exact depends on model size and H100 vs A100 or other hardware.

[19:30] Maya: Are there minimum commitments for Dedicated?
[19:34] Sarah: Minimums depend on capacity. We typically see monthly reserved pools for POCs. We'll propose a small reserved footprint that meets your peak while leaving bursting available.

[20:20] Liam: One of our concerns is unpredictable bursts during events. If we reserve capacity to match average, can Redwood scale quickly to handle 3x spikes?
[20:30] Carlos: Yes — burst capacity is available. There are two mechanisms: short-lived cloud burst (hosted) and pre-warmed burst capacity in Dedicated. There's a cost for burst reservation; we'll model scenarios: reserve for 1.5x average vs require full 3x. Usually a hybrid with targeted burst tickets works.

[21:45] Maya: Regarding fallbacks — if EU dedicated pool is saturated, will requests queue or fail? We prefer failover to a slightly smaller model in-region rather than route out-of-region.
[21:56] Carlos: That's supported via routing policies: can choose 'fail-closed', 'fallback-model-same-region', or 'route-cross-region-with-approval'. We'll recommend fallback to a smaller in-region model to keep residency.

[23:10] Liam: Practical integration timeline for a POC — what's realistic?
[23:16] Sarah: For a basic POC (hosted) with integration and basic evaluation, 2-3 weeks. For Dedicated reserved pool provisioning and pilot, 4-8 weeks depending on contract and capacity. Private/VPC adds another 4-12 weeks depending on networking and compliance reviews.

[24:05] Maya: One final thing — we'd like a token burn forecast per feature so product can decide feature gating. Will you provide a per-route token estimate?
[24:12] Carlos: Yes — the workbook will map routes to expected tokens/day and show how batching/caching affects each route's cost.

[25:00] Liam: About pricing transparency — does Redwood break down token compute vs infra vs orchestration?
[25:06] Sarah: Yes, we provide breakdowns: compute (per-token GPU cycles), networking, storage, and orchestration. You'll get a per-request token cost and also a breakdown so you can do internal chargebacks.

[26:30] Maya: Any gotchas we should know before pilot?
[26:36] Carlos: Watch out for sequence length tail — a few long contexts can blow token budget. Also mixing very different latency classes on the same pool reduces batching efficiency. And quantization can change generation quality; so validate on your eval set.

[27:45] Evelyn: On compliance: do we get penetration test reports and vendor attestations?
[27:51] Sarah: Yes — we'll include SOC 2 report excerpts and a standard security package. For private customers we can do more extensive attestations.

[29:05] Maya: Ok, this helps. One more technical — do you support model pinning per route and version rollouts?
[29:11] Carlos: Absolutely. Model pinning, canary rollouts, A/B, automatic fallback policies all exist in the console. We'll include screenshots and sample rollout configs.

[30:40] Sarah: To recap: we'll send the cost workbook that models hosted vs dedicated vs private for your workload, include batching/kv/quantization scenarios, add latency columns, and attach security docs. We'll also schedule a 60-min technical deep dive next week with your infra and security teams.

[31:00] Maya: Sounds good. Preferred time windows are mornings PST next week.
[31:05] Sarah: Noted. We'll propose options.

[31:40] Liam: Two smaller asks: can you include an example cost plan that assumes a hybrid approach — EU private for regulated customers and hosted for non-EU?
[31:48] Carlos: Yep, we'll include hybrid scenarios with split routing and cost apportionment.

[33:10] Maya: Any immediate blockers from our side? I'll pull together the traffic histogram and sample prompts.
[33:15] Liam: I'll loop in Finance for budget confirmation.
[33:20] Evelyn: I'll sanity-check the KMS and residency requirements and send a short list of required certifications.

[34:00] Sarah: Great. Last quick note — competitors. Maya, you mentioned trying OpenAI and an on-prem vendor; any other constraints vs those providers we should be aware of?
[34:10] Maya: Mainly price and residency. OpenAI had good quality but residency was a problem. Some open-source hosting vendors promised low cost but ops overhead killed the ROI.

[35:00] Carlos: We'll quantify that in the workbook and highlight where Redwood sits relative to hosted API providers vs self-hosted infra.

[36:20] Sarah: Any other questions?
[36:25] Maya: Not for now, thanks.
[36:28] Liam: No.
[36:30] Evelyn: All good.

[36:40] Sarah: Thanks everyone — next steps restated: Sarah will send workbook + security docs; Carlos will prepare microbenchmark data for A100/H100 with batch and quantization permutations; schedule the deep dive.
[36:58] Maya: Thanks Sarah, Carlos.
[37:02] Liam: Thanks.
[37:05] Carlos: Bye all, we'll follow up with proposed slots.

[37:30] Meeting ends.

Notes on transcript quality: occasional word errors (model names and kernel choices slightly garbled), some speaker labels collapsed into names.
